title: Wiggs's own compositions and lead sheets
summary: He names tunes he has written, such as Congo Square and Gallatin Street Grind, and says he copyrights lead sheets.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: They do that sometimes with Bugle Call up north. They thought it was part of Bugle Call. You might make a few remarks about some of the tunes that you've written. The Congo Square. That was your tune, wasn't it?
What are some of the others? I can't think of all of them now.
Gallatin Street Grind. Shepin Tua Joys. Postman's Lament. Well, this thing that Al Rose recorded, he insisted on me using the title Pelican Panic.
Was it something like Canal and Royal?
Oh, yeah. There was a Canal and Royal. And a, there's a, oh goodness, I can't think of them.

I might ask about how you write them. I think we have a couple of sketches that you gave us once that are in the Tulane Library. Or, you know, the little lead sheets and all. Or, how much of that do you write out? Do you write, I forget now, have you had any piano parts written out too? Or, when you copyright them, what do you do?
I just copyright a lead sheet. Just the lead sheet. Most of the time. Sometimes I send a piano part with, but the piano part will be the lead with chords, so it's nothing but a lead sheet.

Because I don't, naturally I'm not going to write a piano part, I'm just going to write the lead with, for the piano player. Yeah. Well, I did most of that arranging at my desk at Warren Easton High School, on the school
I was at WSMB when I arranged most of those things for my band, you see. Yeah. And, uh.
